items.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $F_+,F_-$ be connected compact smooth spanning surfaces for the same nonempty smooth link $L\subset S^3$, equipped with respectively positive and negative definite rational quadratic forms satisfying the normal-transfer linking identity. Suppose their interior intersection is transverse and consists of finitely many embedded circles and properly ending embedded arcs, with the arcs ending only on $L$, and that near $L$ a fixed collar arrangement has already been supplied. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H_t$ of $S^3$, fixed on a neighborhood of $L$, such that the intersection of $H_1(F_+)$ with the original comparison surface $F_-$ has no interior circle components. The arc components and the supplied boundary collar arrangement are unchanged. The endpoint surface $H_1(F_+)$ retains its positive definite normal-transfer form by transport. The finite construction removes at least one circle at each step.

The comparison surface in this statement is held at its original position when intersections are measured; the ambient maps $H_t$ are not required to fix its points.

citations.quote: Assume full AC. Let $F_+,F_-$ be connected compact smooth surfaces embedded in the oriented standard three-sphere, each with nonempty boundary and possibly nonorientable. Supply quadratic forms $q_\pm$ on $H_1(F_\pm;\mathbb Q)$, positive definite and negative definite respectively. Suppose that for every oriented rational multicurve $c$ in the interior of the corresponding surface, $q_\pm[c]=\operatorname{lk}(c,\tau_\pm c)$. Here $\tau_\pm c$ is the cycle obtained by pushing the two-sheeted unit normal line cover of $c$ a sufficiently small distance off that surface, with both sheets oriented by projection to $c$; linking is extended bilinearly over rational coefficients. Let $\gamma$ be a smooth embedded circle in both interiors, and assume their tangent planes are transverse along $\gamma$. Then $\gamma$ bounds a smooth embedded disk in each of $F_+$ and $F_-$. Zero-dimensional first homology is allowed in the definiteness assumptions. The statement makes no assertion that the two disk interiors are mutually disjoint.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: If no circle is present use the identity isotopy. Otherwise [F1] gives disk regions for all the finitely many common circles in $F_-$. Choose one innermost among those disk regions, denoted $D_-$ with boundary $\gamma$. Its interior contains no other circle component. It also contains no arc component: such an arc would have endpoints on $L\subset\partial F_-$ outside this interior disk and would have to cross $\gamma$ to enter it, whereas the transverse intersection components are disjoint. Thus $\operatorname{int}D_-\cap F_+=\varnothing$. Let $D_+\subset F_+$ be its disk from [F1]. For the same reason no intersection arc enters $D_+$. Both disks are disjoint from $L$.

Their interiors are disjoint because $\operatorname{int}D_-$ misses all of $F_+$. Their union is an embedded sphere with one smooth corner circle. Round that corner in its two transverse disk-face charts, inside an arbitrarily small neighborhood of $\gamma$ disjoint from $L$. In the two-dimensional normal cross-section this replaces the two rays by a smooth convex connecting arc and uses its product along $\gamma$; the disk collars give compatible product coordinates. The result is a smooth sphere. Perform the corresponding two-copy disk surgery on $F_+$: remove a thin annular collar of $\gamma$, cap both sides by nearby copies of $D_-$, and round. One component is the sphere $S_0$ just described; the other is a connected surface $F_1$ with boundary $L$, obtained by replacing $D_+$. Choose its cap on the $F_-$ side occupied by $F_+\setminus D_+$ near $\gamma$, with the seam rounded to that same side. Thus this cap and its seam miss $F_-$. They can be taken arbitrarily close to $D_-$ and $\gamma$, so they miss every other intersection component outside $D_+$. The two-copy construction makes $S_0$ and $F_1$ disjoint.

By [F2] and [F5] the sphere $S_0$ bounds two balls. The connected surface $F_1$, disjoint from $S_0$, lies entirely on one side and contains its entire boundary $L$. The opposite ball $V$ therefore misses $F_1$ and $L$. Reversing the two-copy surgery recovers $F_+$ by joining $S_0$ to $F_1$ with a short tube in the chosen product collar. Absorb that short joining collar into $V$ using [F3]. This gives a ball $V'$ whose intersection with $F_1$ is exactly one disk window, and whose interior misses $F_1$ and $L$. Replacing that window by the other boundary disk of $V'$ recovers $F_+$ up to the already arbitrarily small seam choices. All these tracks lie in a neighborhood disjoint from $L$.

This replacement is an isotopy. The ball-window construction in [F3] gives coordinates retaining the window's disk parametrization; flatten one boundary cap in its collar and make the other cap thin by a positive normal rescaling. After rounding the edge, the bulged disk is $t=g(x)$ over a planar disk, with $g\ge0$ smooth and zero near that disk's boundary, and the window is $t=0$. The graphs $t=(1-u)g(x)$ form an isotopy through embedded disks, fixed on a boundary collar, which removes the bulge. Extend it by the identity on the rest of the surface and make it stationary near the time endpoints. To obtain the ambient extension with the asserted support, apply [F4] to a slightly larger disk containing this moving patch and a fixed outer collar. Its track has a neighborhood disjoint from $L$ and from the rest of the surface outside that fixed collar. The extension fixes the collar because the disk isotopy does, and fixes the remaining surface because it lies outside the chosen support. Hence it carries $F_+$ to $F_1$ and is the identity near $L$. No restriction on intersections with the comparison surface during this isotopy is imposed.

At the endpoint the new cap and seam miss $F_-$ by step 2.1. All intersections outside $D_+$ and its small collar are retained. The original circle $\gamma$ and any further circles inside $D_+$ have disappeared, and no arc was changed by step 1.1. Thus the finite circle count strictly decreases, without changing the supplied arrangement near $L$. Transport the form on $F_+$ by the ambient isotopy. It stays positive definite because the induced homology map is an isomorphism, and its normal-transfer linking identity stays valid because an orientation-preserving ambient isotopy transports both the two-sheeted normal push and the linking number; any sufficiently small normal push is homotopic to the transported transverse push in the complement of its underlying cycle. The negative form and the comparison surface are retained in their original position.

Repeat steps 1.1–5.1 with the endpoint surfaces. Their intersection is again the old retained transverse arc and circle family outside the changed disk, with none in the new disk, so the hypotheses for the next step hold. A nonnegative finite integer cannot decrease indefinitely. After at most the original number of circle components this yields a circle-free intersection. Concatenate the finitely many ambient isotopies with stationary time collars. Each fixes a neighborhood of $L$, and their finite common neighborhood is still a neighborhood of $L$; their composition therefore has all the asserted relative and endpoint properties.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 uses the identity when the circle family is empty.
Steps 1.1–5.1 remove at least the selected circle and include a single-circle family.

boundaries.reason: The Statement assumes a finite transverse interior intersection family and fixed smooth boundary collars.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 1.1 and 5.1 keep all intersection arc endpoints and the arrangement near the boundary link unchanged.
Steps 3.1–4.1 explicitly inherit countable choice from full AC for the smooth ball and supported isotopy suppliers.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the opposite-definite common-circle supplier; it implies countable choice for smooth Schoenflies, ball windows and supported isotopy extension.

risk_review.notes: Ball-window graph isotopy and endpoint cap/seam disjointness are explicit in steps2.1–4.1; ambient maps need not fix the comparison surface. Independent owner reading remains owed.

contract.proof_status_evidence: Six literal steps with scoped successful precheck/render/layout; proposed mathematical proof not canonical acceptance.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
**Given:** The objects and hypotheses above.

1.1 Shrink the parametrized ball without collapsing it: $e_t(x)=e(r(t)x)$, where $r$ decreases smoothly from $1$ to a fixed positive $\varepsilon$ and is constant near both ends. Every slice is an embedding. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, its last image lies in one coordinate chart centered at $e(0)$. Write the chart representative of $e$ near $0$ as $f$, with $f(0)=0$ and $L=Df(0)$ invertible. Let $m>0$ satisfy $|Lv|\ge m|v|$. Choose $\varepsilon$ so that $\|Df(y)-L\|<m/2$ for $|y|\le\varepsilon$. The interpolation $f_s(x)=\varepsilon Lx+(1-s)(f(\varepsilon x)-\varepsilon Lx)$ has invertible differential and is injective: its difference from $\varepsilon L$ is Lipschitz with constant less than $\varepsilon m/2$, so $|f_s(x)-f_s(y)|\ge\varepsilon m|x-y|/2$. All images lie in the chart after a further shrink. This is an isotopy from the small ball to a linear ellipsoid. [given, construct]

2.1 Write $L=QP$ with $Q$ orthogonal and $P$ positive definite. The positive definite path $(1-s)P+s\lambda I$, for small $\lambda>0$, gives an isotopy from that ellipsoid to a coordinate round ball. Reparametrize and concatenate the finite paths smoothly with stationary endpoints. By [F1] the resulting embedding isotopy extends to an ambient isotopy carrying $e(D^n)$ to that round ball. A coordinate ball can be moved along any prescribed finite chain of overlapping charts, shrinking it inside each overlap before the next move; a path between its center and any prescribed target center has such a finite chart subdivision. Within a chart, translation and positive dilation of a sufficiently small round ball are embedding isotopies. Hence any two sufficiently small coordinate balls in the same connected component are ambient isotopic. [F1, A1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Parametrize the given $3$-ball $B$ by $D^3$. Its boundary is thereby the standard $S^2$. Apply steps 1.1–2.1 in dimension two to a parametrization of its disk window $W\subset S^2$, then move and enlarge the resulting small round disk to a hemisphere by latitude disks. The endpoint parametrization in step 2.1 is linear orthogonal followed by a positive scalar; its orthogonal factor is the restriction of a fixed orthogonal symmetry of $S^2$. Consequently the standardization can retain the specified disk parametrization, up to that fixed symmetry, rather than only its image. Thus there is an isotopy $h_t$ of $S^2$, starting at the identity, that carries $W$ to a hemisphere, and, if needed, a fixed orthogonal symmetry makes its endpoint agree with the specified standard disk coordinates. This isotopy extends over $D^3$ explicitly: in a radial annulus use $(r,x)\mapsto(r,h_{\alpha(r)t}(x))$, where $\alpha=0$ near the inner edge and $\alpha=1$ near $r=1$, and use the identity on the smaller ball. Each slice is a diffeomorphism, with inverse $(r,y)\mapsto(r,h_{\alpha(r)t}^{-1}(y))$. It is smooth across the inner edge because it is the identity there; the fixed orthogonal symmetry also extends linearly over $D^3$. This proves standardization of the ball-window pair with its disk coordinates, without extending an arbitrary sphere diffeomorphism. [F1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Standardize the added ball's window using its actual attaching parametrization, as permitted by step 3.1. Its collar map is then the product $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t)$ in the receiving disk coordinates. The standard ball-window pair can be represented as a cap over a flat disk: its remaining boundary is a dome meeting the window at its edge. This representation follows by viewing a round ball as two hemispherical graphs and flattening one graph in its collar; the strictly positive normal-coordinate derivative makes the flattening a diffeomorphism. Making the cap thinner is a positive rescaling of its normal coordinate. Therefore in the collar of a disk $D$ in the receiving boundary the attached ball may be represented as a thin cap, with its attaching map retained. A coordinate neighborhood of the whole closed disk exists: extend its full-rank parametrization across the boundary circle using finitely many boundary charts; the extensions agree with it on the disk, and sufficiently small extensions remain injective by compactness and the inverse function theorem. [step 3.1, construct]

5.1 In these coordinates the receiving manifold is $t\ge0$. After rounding the edge, its union with the thin cap is $t\ge\gamma(x)$, where $\gamma\le0$ is smooth and compactly supported in the disk coordinate neighborhood. Take a smooth cutoff $\rho(t)$ equal to one near the cap and zero beyond the chosen receiving collar. Choose the cap thin enough that $\|\gamma\rho'\|_\infty<1$. Then $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t-\gamma(x)\rho(t))$ sends $t\ge\gamma(x)$ diffeomorphically to $t\ge0$: its normal derivative is $1-\gamma(x)\rho'(t)>0$, its boundary value is zero, and it is the identity at the far end of each collar fiber. It is the identity outside this neighborhood, so it pastes to the identity elsewhere. This proves disk absorption. Applying the inverse construction proves disk removal, with the same support assertion. [step 4.1, construct]

6.1 The first assertion is established by steps 1.1–2.1, the window assertion by step 3.1, and both attachment assertions by step 5.1. In particular two balls glued along one boundary disk form a ball; and a boundary-attached ball indented into a ball can be removed leaving a ball. Every use of isotopy extension is in dimensions two or three with compact source and stationary endpoints, as required by [F1]. [F1, A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 5.1] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual steps3.1–5.1 retain window parametrizations and give the flattened thin-cap coordinates used for the graph isotopy, rather than treating a diffeomorphism assertion as an isotopy.
